slices.label: Men outside the South
slices.source: 1910 and 1920 censuses interpolated to November 1912; men 21+ outside the eleven Southern states (including declarant aliens where they could vote); turnout and choice from the backbone, calibrated to certified 1912 returns.

slices.label: Women outside the South
slices.source: 1910 and 1920 censuses interpolated to November 1912; women 21+ outside the South; women could vote for president only in Wyoming, Colorado, Utah, Idaho, Washington (1910) and California (1911); Arizona, Kansas and Oregon adopted suffrage at this same election, so their women first voted for president in 1916.

slices.label: White Southerners
slices.source: 1910 and 1920 censuses interpolated to November 1912; white adults in the eleven former Confederate states (includes a small number of American Indian and Asian adults); calibrated to certified 1912 returns.

slices.label: Black Southerners
slices.source: 1910 and 1920 censuses interpolated to November 1912; Black adults in the eleven former Confederate states; disfranchisement by poll tax, literacy test, grandfather clause and white primary was near complete across the region; the shortfall against white turnout is counted as exclusion.

slices.label: Immigrants not yet citizens
slices.source: 1910 and 1920 censuses interpolated to November 1912; foreign-born white adults who were aliens or had only declared their intent (first papers); declarant aliens could vote in several Midwestern and Western states (fewer each decade as states repealed it), so part of this slice could vote.

runs.summary: Rerun with nothing changed, 1912 comes out as it did: Wilson wins, 435–8–88. The closest state was Arizona, which went to Wilson by 0.2 points. Every one of my 100 reruns reproduces it exactly.
howIGotThis: The numbers: the 1910 and 1920 census counts interpolated to 1912 and certified returns; every draw reproduces 1912 exactly before the change.
How sure: I reran it 100 times with different population and parameter draws.
